title: An average
context: Returns the mean of a list of numbers.

findings.d: `sum =+ v` is `sum = +v`: it keeps only the last value, so the result is silently wrong, never an error. `sum += v`.
`len([])` is 0. Decide what an empty input means (return None, or raise a clear ValueError) and say so.
Inside the function `sum()` no longer works. The whole loop is `sum(values) / len(values)`, or `statistics.mean(values)`.

title: Describing a user
context: `user` is a dict like `{"name": "Asha", "age": 34}`; `name` may be None.

findings.d: `" and " + user["age"]` raises TypeError: Python never converts an int to a string for you (PHP's `.` does). Use an f-string: `f"... {user['age']} years old"`.

findings.t: `status` is unset for anyone 18 or under
findings.d: No `else`, so the variable doesn't exist and you get UnboundLocalError. Give it a value on every path. And check whether 18 itself counts as an adult: `>=`.
None is a single object; compare by identity. `==` can be overridden by a class and linters flag it.
Four `+` and manual spacing. `f"Hello {name}, you are {status} and {age} years old"` is shorter and can't hit the TypeError above.

title: Unique emails
context: Builds a mailing list from user records, one entry per person, in sign-up order.

findings.d: `Asha@x.com` and `asha@x.com` both get in, so the same person is mailed twice. `.strip().lower()` (strictly, only the domain is case-insensitive, but lowering the whole address is the usual choice).

findings.t: `in` on a list is a linear scan
findings.d: Each check walks the whole list: O(n²) for n users. Keep a `set` for the check and the list for order, or `list(dict.fromkeys(emails))`.

findings.t: A missing or None email crashes
findings.d: `u["email"]` raises KeyError and `None.strip()` raises AttributeError. `u.get("email")` and skip empties.

title: Top tags
context: Given a list of posts (dicts from a JSON API), return the `limit` most used tags, case-insensitive.

findings.t: `counts[tag]` on a new key raises KeyError
findings.d: PHP gives null and a notice; Python stops. The first tag ever seen crashes it. Use `counts.get(tag, 0) + 1`, or `collections.Counter`.
That's the method itself, not its result: nothing is lowercased and the keys are method objects. `tag.lower()`.

findings.t: Sorted ascending: returns the least used
findings.d: `sorted` is smallest first. `sorted(..., reverse=True)`, or simply `Counter(...).most_common(limit)`.

findings.t: `post["tags"]` fails on a post without tags
findings.d: API data is often missing keys. `post.get("tags", [])`.
Iterate the list directly: `for post in posts`. The index is never used. Use `enumerate` when it is.

title: Loading a config file
context: Called once at startup to read the app's JSON config.

findings.t: Every error swallowed into an empty config
findings.d: A missing file, broken JSON or bad port all become `{}`, and the app starts with no config. At startup, fail loudly: catch only what you can handle (`FileNotFoundError`, `json.JSONDecodeError`), add context and re-raise.

findings.t: File not closed on the error path
findings.d: If `json.load` raises, `f.close()` never runs. `with open(path, encoding="utf-8") as f:` closes it either way.

findings.t: `print` instead of logging, without the cause
findings.d: "bad config" doesn't say which file or what was wrong. `logger.exception(...)` keeps the traceback.

findings.t: `data["debug"]` crashes when the key is missing
findings.d: And only the string "true" is handled; JSON has real booleans. Validate the whole thing with a Pydantic model (or pydantic-settings) instead of hand-checking keys.
The default depends on the machine's locale. Always pass `encoding="utf-8"` for text files.

title: Retrying a request
context: Fetches JSON from a partner API, retrying when it's flaky.

findings.t: No status check: errors come back as data
findings.d: httpx doesn't raise on 4xx/5xx. A 404 or 500 with a JSON body is returned as if it were the answer. Call `r.raise_for_status()` before `.json()`.
`except Exception` retries a typo, a 401 or a bad URL three times. Retry only what can heal: `httpx.TransportError` (timeouts, resets) and 5xx/429. Let the rest raise at once.
The caller can't tell "failed" from "empty" and will crash later, far from the cause. Re-raise the last error after the final attempt.

findings.t: Fixed one-second wait, even after the last try
findings.d: Every client retries in lockstep, and the last sleep is wasted. Exponential backoff with jitter, and don't sleep after the final attempt.
Lost in production, no level, no traceback. `log.warning(..., exc_info=True)`.

title: A shopping cart class
context: One `Cart` per logged-in user, kept for the length of a request.

findings.d: A class attribute, not one per instance: `self.items.append` mutates the one list, so every user sees everyone's items. Set `self.items = []` in `__init__`, or a dataclass with `field(default_factory=list)`.
`19.99 * 3` isn't exact. Use `Decimal` or integer cents, and round once at the end.
Defining `__eq__` sets `__hash__` to None, so carts can't go in a set or be dict keys. Comparing with a non-Cart raises AttributeError; return `NotImplemented` instead.
`qty=0`, a negative qty or a discount over 100 give zero or negative totals. Check in `add` (or use Pydantic).
A typo like `item["prcie"]` is only found at runtime. A small `@dataclass CartItem` gives names, types and a readable repr.

title: Booking intervals
context: Room bookings. Two bookings clash if their times overlap. Times come from the API with a time zone.

findings.d: Two intervals overlap when *both* hold: `self.start < other.end and other.start < self.end`. With `or`, a booking next month clashes with today's. It's silent and wrong, so it's the worst.

findings.t: `tags: list = []` stops the class from loading
findings.d: dataclasses refuse a mutable default and raise ValueError at import. `tags: list[str] = field(default_factory=list)`.
`timedelta.seconds` is only the part under a day: a 26-hour booking reports 2 hours. `.total_seconds() / 3600`.

findings.t: No check that end is after start
findings.d: A booking that ends before it starts is accepted and breaks `overlaps`. Validate in `__post_init__`.

findings.t: Naive and aware datetimes can't be compared
findings.d: If one side has a time zone and the other doesn't, `<` raises TypeError. Require aware datetimes (and store UTC).

title: Settings and a cache
context: A small helper module imported by several routers.

findings.t: Auth fails open when API_KEY is unset
findings.d: `if not API_KEY or ...` lets everyone in when the env var is missing. Fail closed: refuse to start (or deny) without a key; compare with hmac.compare_digest.
Shared between calls; and `extend` mutates the cached profile, so tags pile up across requests. Default to None and don't mutate shared objects.
Evaluated once, so seen_at never changes. Default to None and compute inside (aware UTC).
Grows forever, never invalidates, differs per worker, and hands one request's mutations to the next. Use a bounded TTL cache or none.
`os.environ.get("DEBUG", True)` is True when unset, and any set string (even "false") is truthy. Parse explicitly, default False (pydantic-settings does this).
Timing leak. Use hmac.compare_digest.

title: Fetching prices
context: Gets current prices for a list of SKUs from the shop's API.

findings.d: `fetch_prices(skus)` in a plain `def` returns a coroutine object, never run; `prices[sku]` raises TypeError and Python warns "never awaited". Make `price_report` async and `await` it (or `asyncio.run` at the very top).
Awaiting in a loop is sequential: 100 SKUs, 100 round trips. `asyncio.gather(...)`, bounded by an `asyncio.Semaphore` so the shop isn't flooded.
A 404 or 500 has no `price`, so it surfaces as a KeyError. `r.raise_for_status()`, and decide what a missing SKU means.
The loop holds only a weak reference: the task can be garbage-collected mid-flight, and its exceptions are never seen. Keep a reference (a set), or use `asyncio.TaskGroup`.

title: Checking many URLs
context: A nightly job checks up to 20,000 customer URLs and reports each one's status.
code:
import asyncio, httpx

async def check_all(urls):
    async with httpx.AsyncClient(timeout=5) as client:
        results = await asyncio.gather(*[client.get(u) for u in urls])
    return {u: r.status_code for u, r in zip(urls, results)}

findings.t: One failure throws away every result
findings.d: `gather` raises the first exception, and the 19,999 other answers are lost. One dead host is guaranteed in 20,000. `return_exceptions=True` and report errors per URL, or catch inside a small per-URL function.

20,000 coroutines start at once. httpx's pool holds 100 connections, so the rest queue, and the 5 s timeout includes waiting for a connection: healthy sites time out. Use an `asyncio.Semaphore` (say 50) around each request.
httpx doesn't follow redirects by default, so every site that moved to https reports 301. `follow_redirects=True` if you want the final status.

findings.t: Duplicate URLs collapse in the dict
findings.d: If the list repeats a URL, the dict keeps only the last result. De-duplicate first, or return a list of pairs.

findings.t: Everything is held in memory until the end
findings.d: No progress, and a crash at 19,000 loses it all. Process in batches (or `asyncio.as_completed`) and write results as they come.

title: Creating a user
context: Sign-up endpoint. `UserRow` is the SQLAlchemy model with the same columns.

findings.t: The password is stored as plain text
findings.d: `model_dump()` copies `password` straight into the row. Hash it (argon2 or bcrypt) and store only the hash: `UserRow(**user.model_dump(exclude={"password"}), password_hash=hash_pw(user.password))`.

findings.t: `UserOut` inherits the password, so it's sent back
findings.d: The response model is the filter, and this one lets the password through. Build `UserOut` from a shared base without it: `UserBase` → `UserIn(UserBase)` + password, `UserOut(UserBase)` + id.

findings.t: The client chooses its own role
findings.d: Mass assignment: send `"role": "admin"` and you are one. Leave `role` out of the input model; the server sets it.
Any string is an email, any int an age (−5, 10⁹). `EmailStr`, `Field(ge=13, le=130)`, a minimum password length. A duplicate email is also a 500; catch IntegrityError and return 409.

title: Creating a device
context: Clients register a device they own. `DeviceRow` is the SQLAlchemy model; `serial` is unique in the table.
code:
class Device(BaseModel):
    serial: str
    owner_email: str
    notes: str = None
    is_admin_device: bool = False

@app.post("/devices")
def create_device(device: Device, db: DB):
    row = DeviceRow(**device.dict())
    db.add(row)
    db.commit()
    return row

findings.d: Everything in the model goes straight into the row, so anyone can register an admin device. Split models: `DeviceIn` with only what a client may send, the server sets the rest.
Returning the ORM row exposes every column (now and any added later). `response_model=DeviceOut`.
The unique constraint raises IntegrityError. Catch it, roll back, return 409.
`@app.post(..., status_code=201)`.
`notes: str = None` should be `str | None = None`. `serial` can be empty and `owner_email` anything: `Field(min_length=1, max_length=64)`, `EmailStr`.
Deprecated in v2: `model_dump()`.

title: Admin dependencies
context: Admins can delete users. Clients send their token in a `token` header.

findings.d: For a non-admin it returns None and the route runs anyway: anyone with a token can delete users. `raise HTTPException(403)`; a dependency stops a request only by raising.
`return` instead of `yield`: nothing closes the session, connections leak until the pool runs out. `db = SessionLocal(); try: yield db; finally: db.close()`.
`current_user` returns None, then `user.role` raises AttributeError. Raise 401 there.

findings.t: Deleting a missing user says it worked
findings.d: Check the row count (or fetch first) and return 404.
`admin = Depends(...)` hides what it is. `admin: Annotated[User, Depends(require_admin)]` (or a type alias) makes it readable and checkable.

title: Signup with a welcome email
context: `DB` is a sync SQLAlchemy session; `hash_pw` is argon2 (about 100 ms of CPU); `send_welcome_email` talks SMTP and takes about 2 s.
code:
@app.post("/signup", status_code=201)
async def signup(body: SignupIn, db: DB, background: BackgroundTasks):
    user = User(email=body.email, password_hash=hash_pw(body.password))
    db.add(user)
    db.commit()
    send_welcome_email(user.email)
    background.add_task(sync_to_crm, user)
    return {"id": user.id}

findings.d: Two seconds where the event loop serves nobody else on that worker. Send it as a background task (or queue it), and don't block in async code.

findings.t: Sync DB and CPU-heavy hashing in `async def`
findings.d: These block the loop too. With a sync session, make the endpoint plain `def` so FastAPI runs it in the threadpool.

findings.t: ORM object handed to a background task
findings.d: The task runs after the response, when the request's session is closed: lazy loads fail or the data is stale. Pass `user.id` and load it in the task.
Unique constraint → IntegrityError. Roll back and return 409.
If SMTP fails the client gets a 500 though the account exists, retries, and hits the duplicate. Side effects go after the response (or in an outbox).

title: An async report
context: Fetches the status of each of a customer's devices from a vendor API and returns a summary.

findings.d: requests.get, time.sleep and the sync DB call all block the event loop: one slow report stalls every request on the worker. Use httpx.AsyncClient and asyncio.sleep (and an async DB), or make the handler plain `def`.

findings.t: No timeout on the vendor call
findings.d: requests has no default timeout; a hung vendor hangs the request (and with the bug above, the worker). Always pass a timeout.
Vendor errors, JSON errors and typos all vanish; the report silently omits devices. Catch httpx/requests errors, log them, and mark the device as unknown.
N devices × (latency + 0.1 s). With an async client, run them concurrently with asyncio.gather and a semaphore to stay polite.
Anyone can request any customer's report (IDOR). Depend on the current user and check ownership.
Server-local time with no zone. Use `datetime.now(timezone.utc)`.

title: Uploading an avatar
context: Users upload a profile picture. `static/` is served from the same domain as the app.
code:
@app.post("/avatar")
async def upload_avatar(file: UploadFile, user: CurrentUser):
    data = await file.read()
    path = f"static/avatars/{file.filename}"
    with open(path, "wb") as f:
        f.write(data)
    user.avatar = path
    return {"url": "/" + path}

findings.d: The filename comes from the client. `../../app/main.py` overwrites your code. Never use it for the path: generate one (`f"{uuid4().hex}.png"`).

findings.t: Any file type, served from your domain
findings.d: An `.html` or `.svg` file with script in it runs as your site (stored XSS). Check the real type (open it with Pillow), allow only images, re-encode, and serve uploads from a separate domain.
Two people uploading `me.jpg` share one file. The generated name above fixes this too.

findings.t: No size limit; it's all read into memory
findings.d: `await file.read()` on a 2 GB upload. Cap the size (at the proxy and in the code) and stream to disk in chunks.
No session, no commit: the change vanishes with the request. And `open`/`write` in `async def` block the event loop; use plain `def` or run them in a thread.

title: A login endpoint
context: Users log in with email and password and get a token for the API. Assume `db`, `User` and `SECRET` exist.

findings.d: Fast and unsalted, so leaked hashes are cracked in bulk. Use a slow, salted hash (argon2 via pwdlib, or bcrypt) and its verify function.
`"user": user` serialises every column, password_hash included. Add a response model (UserOut) with only safe fields.

findings.t: Different errors reveal which emails exist
findings.d: 404 "no such user" vs 401 "wrong password" lets anyone enumerate accounts. Return the same 401 for both.
No `exp` claim: a leaked token works forever. Add `exp` and decode with explicit `algorithms=[...]`.
`random` is predictable. Use `secrets.token_urlsafe(32)`.
Simple-typed params are query params, so the password lands in URLs and access logs. Take a Pydantic body (or OAuth2 form) instead. Also: no rate limit on login.

title: A payment webhook
context: The payment provider POSTs events, signed with HMAC-SHA256 of the raw body in `X-Signature`. It retries anything that isn't 2xx, and may deliver an event twice.
code:
@app.post("/webhooks/payments")
async def payment_webhook(request: Request, db: DB):
    body = await request.json()
    sig = request.headers.get("X-Signature")
    expected = hmac.new(SECRET, json.dumps(body).encode(), "sha256").hexdigest()
    if sig != expected:
        raise HTTPException(401)
    order = db.get(Order, body["order_id"])
    order.status = "paid"
    db.commit()
    return {"ok": True}

findings.t: Every signed event marks the order paid
findings.d: The event type and amount are never checked: a `payment.failed` or a refund, correctly signed, sets status to paid. Check `body["type"]`, the amount and the currency against the order.

findings.t: Signs re-serialised JSON, not the raw body
findings.d: `json.dumps(body)` won't match the provider's bytes (spacing, key order, unicode escapes), so real events fail, and the usual "fix" is to turn the check off. HMAC `await request.body()`, then parse.
The provider may send the same event twice, and a captured request can be replayed forever. Store processed event ids (unique column) and reject old timestamps if the provider signs one.
Use `hmac.compare_digest(sig or "", expected)`. A missing header is also None here.

findings.t: An unknown order is a 500, retried forever
findings.d: `db.get` returns None, then `.status` crashes. The provider retries for days. Log it and return 2xx (or 404) deliberately.
The sync session blocks the event loop while it waits on Postgres. Keep `async def` for reading the raw body and run the DB part with `run_in_threadpool`, or use an async session.

title: A paged list
context: Lists products 20 at a time. The UI asks for `page=1` first. The table has 2 million rows.

findings.t: Loads the whole table to return 20 rows
findings.d: `.all()` pulls 2 million rows into memory on every request, then slices in Python. Page in SQL: `.offset((page - 1) * size).limit(size)`.
Pages start at 1 but `start = page * size`, so the first 20 products are never shown. `(page - 1) * size`.
Without ORDER BY the database may return rows in any order, so items repeat or vanish between pages. `.order_by(Product.id)` (or a column plus the id as a tie-break).
`size=1000000` or `page=-3` are accepted. `Query(ge=1, le=100)` and `Query(ge=1)`. For deep pages, keyset paging (`WHERE id > last_id`) beats a large OFFSET.

title: Listing orders
context: Returns a user's orders with item counts, optionally sorted by a column the client chooses.

findings.d: `sort` is pasted into the SQL. Identifiers can't be bound parameters, so map it through an allow-list: `{"created_at": Order.created_at, ...}[sort]`, else 422.
`db = SessionLocal()` is shared by all requests and threads; one error poisons it for everyone. Use a per-request session via Depends(get_db) with yield.
Any caller can list any user's orders. Derive the user from auth, or check `user_id == current_user.id`.
One get() and one lazy load of items per row. Query Orders with `selectinload(Order.items)` (or a COUNT with GROUP BY).
Returns every order ever. Add limit/offset with a capped maximum.
`float(order.total)` introduces rounding errors. Keep Decimal and serialise as a string, or use integer cents.

title: Importing readings
context: Devices send batches of meter readings as JSON. `SessionLocal = sessionmaker(engine)`; `Reading.device_id` is NOT NULL.
code:
def import_readings(rows):
    saved = []
    for row in rows:
        session = SessionLocal()
        device = session.scalar(select(Device).where(Device.serial == row["serial"]))
        reading = Reading(device=device, value=row["value"], taken_at=row["taken_at"])
        session.add(reading)
        session.commit()
        saved.append(reading)
    return saved

@app.post("/readings/import")
def import_endpoint(rows: list[dict]):
    saved = import_readings(rows)
    return [{"id": r.id, "device": r.device.serial} for r in saved]

findings.t: A commit per row: not atomic
findings.d: Row 300 fails and 299 are already committed; the client retries and they're duplicated. One transaction for the batch: `with SessionLocal.begin() as session:` and `add_all`.
`SessionLocal()` without `with` or `close()`: each one keeps a pooled connection until garbage collection. A big import exhausts the pool ("QueuePool limit reached") and every other request waits.
`device` is None, the NOT NULL `device_id` fails at commit with IntegrityError. Look the serials up first and return 422 naming the unknown ones.

findings.t: The response reloads every row, twice
findings.d: After commit each reading is expired: `r.id` is a SELECT, `r.device` a lazy load: 2N queries. It only works because the sessions leaked; close them and it's DetachedInstanceError. Build the response inside the session (after a flush the ids are there).
N SELECTs for the serials. Load them in one: `select(Device).where(Device.serial.in_(serials))`, into a dict.
A missing `value` is a KeyError (500); a string value goes straight to the database. A Pydantic `ReadingIn` model gives a 422 with the field, and a size limit on the batch.

title: Caching the current user
context: To save a query per request, the token lookup is cached. Runs under 4 uvicorn workers. Clients send `Authorization: Bearer <token>`.

findings.d: The cache never expires: after logout, a ban or a role change, the old token still returns the old user, in each of 4 workers separately. Cache with a short TTL in a shared store (Redis) and delete on logout, or don't cache auth at all.
`user` came from another, closed session, so it's detached: `db` doesn't track it and the commit writes nothing. Load the user in `db` (`db.get(User, user.id)`) or `db.merge(user)`, then change it.

findings.t: One User object shared by every request
findings.d: The cached instance is returned to every request with that token, on every thread. A change made in one request leaks into others, and lazy-loaded attributes raise DetachedInstanceError.
A database leak hands over every live session. Store a hash of the token (SHA-256 is fine for random tokens) and look up by the hash.

findings.t: A missing or malformed header is a 422, not a 401
findings.d: `Header()` makes it required, so FastAPI answers 422. `removeprefix` also accepts a token without `Bearer`. Use `HTTPBearer`, which returns 401/403 properly.

title: Product search
context: A search box on the shop. Each product has a category (a relationship). Postgres.

findings.t: N+1: one query per product's category
findings.d: `p.category` lazy-loads, so 500 results are 501 queries. `.options(selectinload(Product.category))` (or joinedload).
`q=a` matches most of the table and returns it all. `.limit(50)` and paging.

findings.t: `%` and `_` in the search act as wildcards
findings.d: Not SQL injection: the value is bound as a parameter, so calling it injection would be wrong. But `q=%` matches everything. `Product.name.contains(q, autoescape=True)` escapes them.
A leading wildcard means a full table scan each keystroke. A trigram index (pg_trgm) or full-text search.
`like` is case-sensitive there, so `shoe` misses `Shoe`. `ilike` (which also needs the trigram index to be fast). And require a minimum length for `q`.

title: Transferring credit
context: Moves credit between two accounts the caller owns.

findings.d: If the second update fails, the debit is committed and the credit isn't. Do both in one transaction (`with db.begin():`).
Read-check-write in Python: two concurrent transfers both see enough balance. Lock rows (`with_for_update()`) or update atomically with a `balance >= amount` condition and check the row count.
`user` is never used: anyone can move anyone's money. Load accounts filtered by owner_id.
A negative amount moves money the other way. `amount: Decimal = Field(gt=0)` in TransferIn. Also from_id == to_id.
db.get returns None for unknown ids, then `.balance` raises AttributeError. Return 404.
Insufficient funds returns 200 with ok: false. Use 409 (or 422) via HTTPException.

title: A job queue in a table
context: Several worker processes run this loop against the same Postgres table of jobs.

findings.t: Two workers claim the same job
findings.d: Both SELECT the same pending row before either commits, so the job runs twice (two emails, two charges). `.with_for_update(skip_locked=True)` on the select, or one `UPDATE ... WHERE id = (SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED) RETURNING`.

findings.t: A crashed worker leaves jobs running forever
findings.d: If the process dies mid-job, nothing ever resets the row. Store a lease (`locked_until`) and let other workers reclaim expired ones; make `handle` safe to run twice.

findings.t: A DB error inside `handle` breaks the loop
findings.d: If `handle` uses this session and a statement fails, the session needs a rollback; `db.commit()` then raises PendingRollbackError and the worker dies. `db.rollback()` in the except before recording the failure.

findings.t: Failures are recorded without a reason or a retry
findings.d: `except Exception` drops the error. Save the message, count attempts, and retry with backoff up to a limit.

findings.t: One session for the worker's whole life
findings.d: Its identity map keeps every job it has touched. A session per job (`with SessionLocal() as db:`) keeps memory flat and failures contained.

findings.t: No index for the claim query
findings.d: Every poll scans for pending rows. An index on `(status, created_at)`, ideally partial: `WHERE status = 'pending'`.

title: Tests for a discount helper
context: `apply_discount(price, percent)` should raise ValueError for a percent outside 0–100.

findings.d: `assert False` raises AssertionError, which `except Exception` catches: it passes even when no error is raised. `with pytest.raises(ValueError, match="percent"):` (PHPUnit's `expectException`).
`19.99 * 0.85` isn't exactly 16.9915. `pytest.approx(...)`, or better, money in Decimal or cents.
Passes alone, fails when another test touches it or it runs twice. Give each test its own data with a fixture.
The first failing assert hides the rest. `@pytest.mark.parametrize` (PHPUnit's data providers) runs and reports each case.
100%, just over 100, rounding to cents: where the bugs are. And a failure message per case comes free with parametrize.

title: A test file
context: Tests for a certificate-expiry endpoint that also calls a vendor revocation API.
code:
from fastapi.testclient import TestClient
from app.main import app, get_db
import time
from datetime import datetime, timedelta

client = TestClient(app)
app.dependency_overrides[get_db] = lambda: test_session

def test_expiring_soon():
    cert = make_cert(not_after=datetime.now() + timedelta(days=1))
    r = client.get(f"/certs/{cert.serial}")
    assert r.status_code == 200

def test_revoked():
    r = client.get("/certs/REVOKED-1")      # real vendor API
    time.sleep(2)                           # wait for vendor
    assert r.json()["revoked"] is True

findings.d: Flaky, slow and dependent on the network and vendor data. Override the HTTP client dependency with httpx.MockTransport.
`datetime.now()` (naive, local) plus a 1-day window breaks near midnight or across zones. Inject a fixed aware `now`.
test_expiring_soon never checks the expiry flag or days left: it passes even if the logic is wrong. Assert the body.

findings.t: Overrides set globally and never cleared
findings.d: Set at import and leaked into every other test file. Use a fixture that sets and clears `dependency_overrides`.
The request already completed; sleeping only slows the suite. With a fake transport there's nothing to wait for.
TestClient outside a `with` block doesn't run lifespan, so startup-created clients and engines don't exist. Use `with TestClient(app) as client` in a fixture.
